On Sunday, South Korea's finance minister called the central bank chief and three top regulators into an emergency meeting in Seoul. The goal was to stop a "Black Monday" before markets opened.

China and Taiwan moved too. But the money at risk reaches far beyond Asia. The S&P 500 enters Monday on seven straight losses, its longest run since February 2020.

Asia's Rescue Plan Has a Weak Record

China will let investors borrow more to buy stocks, freeing an estimated 400 billion yuan, per The Standard. It starts November 30, a week after Monday.

"The fund is a good booster right now, but I doubt it changes the trend," the Korea Times noted, citing Floodlines Research founder Anna Wu.

Why Wall Street Can't Ignore Asia

Both markets run on the same AI chip trade. Nvidia fell 14% on Friday, and AMD's five-day slide topped 24%.

"This is not a fatal illness. It's not even the flu," he said.

title: Why York Space Systems Stock Plunged This Week
detail:
Why York Space Systems Stock Plunged This Week
Scott Levine, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 1:54 PM MST 4 min read
YSS
^GSPC
Trade YSS on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

A wave of Wall Street price-target cuts following government contract delays sent York Space Systems (NYSE:YSS) tumbling 36.9% this week, according to data provided by S&P Global Market Intelligence.

York Space Systems stock changed hands at $3.65 as of the close on Friday, Nov. 20, down 36.9% from Friday, Nov. 13's close. Across those five sessions, the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) fell 5.1%, and the Nasdaq-100 was down 5.1%.

Image source: Getty Images.

Wall Street slashes price targets after contract delays

Analyst downgrades and price-target reductions hit the defense hardware provider throughout the week. Barclays cut its price target from $11 to $5, while JPMorgan lowered its target from $17 to $7. The reductions followed the company's third-quarter report, in which management revealed a $749.7 million goodwill impairment charge due to delayed government contract awards. The stock is down 92% (as of the close on Friday, Nov. 20) from its 52-week high of $44.54.

York Space Systems manufactures small satellites and ground communications equipment for military, civil, and commercial space operators. It builds platforms like the Tranche 0 satellite line and Hydra MAX communications terminals used by national security agencies. The stock trades below $5, but the company generated $84.2 million in revenue last quarter from its spacecraft and ground hardware.

Management also announced plans to acquire Australian ground robotics maker Outlook Industries to expand into unmanned terrestrial defense systems. The deal expands York's total addressable market by $3.1 billion, but investors remained focused on near-term balance-sheet pressure. Wall Street's sharp price-target cuts invert the growth story, forcing investors to weigh a major impairment and defense contract delays against new expansion plans.

What's next for York Space Systems

York ended the quarter with $308.9 million in cash and short-term investments as of Sept. 30, 2026, against $179.8 million in total debt, including lease obligations. While the company holds a $14.9 billion pipeline of government opportunities, contract timing remains unpredictable. Investors will look to the closing of the Outlook acquisition and upcoming defense contract decisions in early 2027 to see if revenue growth recovers.

Is York Space Systems stock a buy?

York Space Systems stock is available for a fraction of what it cost last spring when it was changing hands at north of $45.

While York Space Systems claims it has a nearly $15 billion pipeline of government opportunities, there's no certainty that it will convert this to backlog -- and ultimately concrete sales. Take this, along with the fact that the company is burning through an increasing amount of cash -- operating cash flow through the first nine months of 2026 totaled $248.4 million compared to $88.2 million during the same period in 2025 -- and it seems that those seeking a compelling space stock opportunity now would be better off looking somewhere else.

Bridgewater Associates, the macro fund founded by Ray Dalio, disclosed in a 13F filing on November 16, 2026, that it held 16.3% of its reported $23 billion U.S. stock portfolio in two S&P 500 index funds as of September 30, 2026.

websummit / Flickr

Those two funds were the SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) and the iShares Core S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA:IVV). Bridgewater kept that stake even after selling a large block of both during the quarter. A smaller position in the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF (NYSEARCA:VOO) brought total S&P 500 fund exposure to 16.5%.

A Famous Macro Fund's Largest Holding Is the Index Itself

SPY was Bridgewater's largest reported position, valued at $2,595,471,644, or about 11.3% of the portfolio. IVV ranked second at $1,154,942,390, or about 5.0%. During the quarter, Bridgewater sold 1,916,991 SPY shares and 1,494,233 IVV shares, which left 3,403,317 and 1,508,053 shares, respectively. The fund reduced its index allocation during the quarter. Even after that reduction, broad market exposure stayed the core of its reported equity book.

Nvidia Was Trimmed Too

NVIDIA (NASDAQ:NVDA) was the third-largest position, at $613,935,912. Bridgewater sold 1,177,974 shares and ended the quarter with 2,688,221. The index funds also add to that exposure. Nvidia was SPY's largest holding at 7.58% of net assets as of March 17, 2026, so anyone who owns the S&P 500 also owns a meaningful amount of Nvidia.

Volatility in the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) has picked up since the midterm elections. That week was the index's worst since April 2025, and it now sits roughly 10% below its all-time high.

That kind of volatility doesn't usually happen when the S&P 500 is near its all-time highs. It's often considered a sign that the conditions that lifted stock prices to records may no longer be in place. And investors are dealing with some real concerns about where the market heads from here.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

While bounces like the one that took place the week ending Nov. 13 might feel like relief, history shows that might not be the case.

Image source: Getty Images.

This setup tends to produce weaker forward-looking returns

I went back and looked at S&P 500 history since 1970. Specifically, I looked for periods of market swings that look just like the one we experienced. Over history, there were 19 instances in which the index fell by at least 2.5% one week and rebounded by more than 2.5% the next week, while still within reach of an all-time high.

The good news is that recent history has shown solid gains for the S&P 500 following these periods. Since 2018, all six occurrences produced positive returns six months later, with a median return of more than 11%.

The bad news is that prior to that, the results are incredibly mixed. There are more instances of negative forward returns, and the gains six months later were often minimal. Plus, some of these examples came during some of history's worst bear markets.

title: Here Are the 4 Investing Rules I'm Never Breaking, No Matter How Scary the Stock Market Gets
detail:
Here Are the 4 Investing Rules I'm Never Breaking, No Matter How Scary the Stock Market Gets
James Brumley, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 11:05 AM MST 6 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

It remains to be seen whether the market's due for any further downside. But there's certainly no denying it's possible.

As scary as the past few weeks have been, from peak to trough the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) has only tumbled about 7%, leaving it shy of the minimum sell-off of 10% just to qualify as an ordinary correction. Given that we're overdue for such a move, the pullback from October's peak so far still feels like it could continue unfurling. Plenty of investors, including me, are understandably concerned.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Nevertheless, I've been in and around this business long enough to know there are just some things I and every other investor should make a point of doing no matter how scary things get. Here's a rundown of my four non-negotiable rules for surviving market setbacks, and for that matter, thriving during bullish periods.

It will come as no surprise that all four are so well-preached that they've almost become cliché. There's a good reason for that, however.

1. Stick with quality companies

As legendary investor Warren Buffett put it, "it's far better to buy a wonderful company at a fair price than a fair company at a wonderful price." This simply means that your priority should be owning quality investments even if it means paying a premium for them. In the long run, quality ends up paying for itself. Or as the antithesis adage goes, "cheap stocks are cheap for a reason."

This idea is likely to give many investors more than a little pause here. Now three years into a bull market that's been led by AI-mania (which has also in turn drawn out some very speculative IPOs), it's going to be tough for most people to admit they've taken on some risk that's more rooted in hope than actual opportunity. It happens.

The good news is that any major reset for the market should jolt everyone -- and valuations -- back to more historically sustainable norms.

2. Pick stocks with an intended time frame in mind

Most everyone has a basic time frame in mind when they're investing. For most of us, it ends with retirement, when we're all likely to dramatically reshape our portfolios for reliable income rather than growth.

If we're being intellectually honest with ourselves, however, all of us are probably at least a little bit guilty of scooping up the occasional name that's not actually aligned with our target time frame. We're attracted by the buzzy bullish rhetoric, and dive in expecting above-average gains in a below-average amount of time. And that's OK. Again, it happens.

title: The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Are Dangerously Close to Joining the Nasdaq in a Correction. Here’s the Level That Would Put the Nasdaq in a Bear Market, and What History Says Investors Should Do During a Stock Market Crash.
detail:
The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Are Dangerously Close to Joining the Nasdaq in a Correction. Here’s the Level That Would Put the Nasdaq in a Bear Market, and What History Says Investors Should Do During a Stock Market Crash.
Daniel Foelber, The Motley Fool
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 10:50 AM MST 7 min read
^IXIC
^GSPC
^DJI
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The stock market sell-off has gone from bad to worse, with ripple effects extending to the major indexes.

The Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) is now firmly in a correction, which is a drop of at least 10% from this high. As of Nov. 19 market close, the Dow Jones Industrial Average (DJINDICES:^DJI) is down 9.7% from its high, while the S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) has proven more resilient but is still down 8.2% from its highs. It's worth mentioning that the Nasdaq and S&P 500 were both at all-time highs in early October -- showcasing the speed and severity of the sell-off.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Here's the level that the Nasdaq would need to reach to be in bear market territory, the differences between a stock market crash and a bear market, and how to navigate further volatility.

Image source: Getty Images.

22,178.20 in the Nasdaq Composite would mark a 20% decline

The Nasdaq Composite closed at 23,879.20 on Nov. 19 -- putting it 13.5% off its all-time high.

^SPX data by YCharts

If the Nasdaq fell to 22,178.20, that would put the index down 20% from its all-time high of 27,722.75, set on Oct. 6.

A bear market is defined as a prolonged downturn of at least 20% from a high. So, for example, the rapid sell-off during the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic in March 2020 and the tariff-induced sell-off in April 2025 both saw the Nasdaq down over 20% from its high, but those levels were very short-lived. In contrast, the broader sell-off in growth stocks during 2022, when the Nasdaq fell 33%, was a legitimate bear market.

A stock market crash is typically defined as a sudden drop in a major index. Exact definitions vary based on speed and severity. For example, a 10% drop in a week can feel more crash-like than a 20% drop over six months, even if the 20% drop is more damaging to your portfolio. However, if the Nasdaq does fall to that 20% drawdown level over the next few weeks, I think it's fair to call it a crash, given that the all-time high occurred just six weeks ago. And the speed of the sell-off, especially over the last couple of weeks, has been rapid. Especially in certain sectors.

Nvidia is down 32.3% in three weeks

There are already pockets of the stock market that have undergone crash-like sell-offs. In just three weeks, the Nasdaq Composite is down 10.1%. Even gold and Bitcoin (CRYPTO:BTC) have undergone rapid declines. Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), which was the world's most valuable company for most of this year, has lost roughly a third of its value in three weeks -- accelerated by the sudden resignation of its founder and CEO of over 33 years, Jensen Huang.

title: Gold Is Crashing Like 2008. Peter Schiff Says That's Exactly Why He's Bullish
detail:
Gold Is Crashing Like 2008. Peter Schiff Says That's Exactly Why He's Bullish
Lockridge Okoth
Sun, November 22, 2026 at 10:51 AM MST 2 min read
GC=F
^GSPC
Gold Falls to Its Lowest Point of 2026: Analysts Weigh In. Photo by BeInCrypto

Gold fell 8.9% last week to close near $3,538 an ounce, a level last seen in September 2025. Peter Schiff says the slide mirrors 2008, when gold crashed just before it nearly tripled.

The metal now trades more than a third below its January record above $5,600. Owners of bullion, gold funds, and mining stocks have taken those losses as traders bet the Federal Reserve will raise rates again on Dec. 9.

What Happened to Gold After the 2008 Crash?

Schiff, an economist and longtime gold advocate, laid out the comparison on his weekly podcast. In 2008, he said, gold peaked early in the year and slid for months before Wall Street broke.

When stocks collapsed that fall, gold initially dropped harder. However, the metal bottomed in late 2008, while the S&P 500 kept sinking until March 2009, Schiff said.

Gold then climbed from about $681 to roughly $1,921 by September 2011, a 183% gain, TradingView chart data shows. That rally followed Fed rate cuts to near zero and bond buying with newly created money.

Gold Price Performance in 2008. Source: TradingView
Who Is Selling Gold, According to Peter Schiff?

Schiff blames forced selling. Traders who borrowed to bet on gold futures face margin calls, demands for extra cash that push them to dump positions.

Meanwhile, big buyers such as central banks are waiting for the selling to end, he argued. He also said online dealers now charge $10 to $15 above market prices for silver coins.

Schiff runs SchiffGold, a precious metals dealer he promoted during the same episode.

"I think the gold and silver traders are right to know that there is a crisis coming. They've just got the wrong outcome," he said.

Is a Fed Pivot Coming Soon Enough?

Schiff expects a Fed pivot, meaning a turn away from rate hikes, to start gold's next rally. He has argued that a hard tightening cycle would crash stocks, bonds, and housing.

Goldman Sachs sees a longer road. Its economists expect hikes in December and March 2027, with gold reclaiming $5,600 only in 2028.

The Dec. 9 decision is the next test. In 2008, the Fed reversed only after markets broke, which is the sequence Schiff says is repeating.
